title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
hook: Robot policies mostly look at the last step or two. NVIDIA's RoboTTT pushes visuomotor context to 8,000 timesteps without slowing inference — and finds performance keeps climbing the whole way.
key_points: Most robot foundation models condition on single-step or short-history visual input; RoboTTT scales context to 8K timesteps, three orders of magnitude further, without added inference latency.
It folds Test-Time Training into the policy: 'fast weights' updated by gradient descent compress history into weight space, both during training and at inference.
Training recipe combines sequence action forcing with truncated backpropagation through time to make the long context trainable.
At 8K-timestep context, the model beats its own 1K-timestep version by 62% and the single-step baseline by 87% on real-robot manipulation.
Unlocks one-shot imitation from human video, on-the-fly policy improvement, and completing a 5-minute, 10-stage assembly task no baseline finished.
content_html:
Robot foundation models have mostly been stuck looking at the current frame or a short window before it. A team including NVIDIA's GEAR lab (Yunfan Jiang, Linxi "Jim" Fan, and collaborators including Li Fei-Fei and Yuke Zhu) pushes that window out to 8,000 timesteps with RoboTTT — three orders of magnitude beyond prior policies — while keeping inference speed flat.

The trick is Test-Time Training: instead of attending over a growing sequence, RoboTTT compresses history into a set of "fast weights" that get updated by gradient descent both while training and while the robot is acting, then retrieves from that compressed state for long-context conditioning. To make training over such long context tractable, they combine sequence action forcing with truncated backpropagation through time. The payoff, per the paper: 87% better performance than a single-step baseline, a 62% jump over their own 1K-timestep version, one-shot imitation from human video, and completion of a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task that no baseline managed. The authors frame context length itself as a new scaling axis for robot policies, alongside model size and data. Videos and details are linked via the source.
extra_html: This work sits alongside a broader trend of bringing test-time training into agentic and embodied systems — using update-time compute, not just more parameters, to adapt to what's happening right now. Full paper and demo videos are linked via the source.

related.title: Agentic Test-Time Training: Adapting Mid-Episode
related.hook: LLM agents degrade over long episodes, repeating failed moves — this method updates the model's weights continuously during the episode itself, but only on genuinely new information.

related.title: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Model
related.hook: π0 is a generalist robot policy: it takes camera images, joint angles, and a plain-language instruction, and outputs smooth action sequences — folding laundry, bussing tables, bagging groceries.

flashcards.prompt: How does RoboTTT scale a robot policy's context to 8K timesteps without growing inference latency?
flashcards.back_html: It uses Test-Time Training: a recurrent 'fast weights' state, updated by gradient descent during both training and inference, compresses long history into weight space instead of a growing token sequence.

flashcards.prompt: What did RoboTTT observe as pretraining context length scaled up, for the first time in this line of work?

choices.text: Steady gains in closed-loop performance as context length increased
Inference latency grew linearly with context length
Longer context only helped on tasks under one stage

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors report steady closed-loop performance gains as context scales, framing context length itself as a new scaling axis for robot foundation models — the 8K-context model beat the 1K-context version by 62%.

flashcards.prompt: Name two new robot capabilities RoboTTT's long context unlocks.
flashcards.back_html: One-shot in-context imitation from human video demonstrations, and on-the-fly policy improvement — plus better robustness to perturbations and long-horizon, multi-stage tasks.
